7d104a7a451af59878d3d8cdf441962e.text: Fill shoe boxes with toys, cloths and craft supplies to children overseas this Christmas through Evangelical Free Church for this year’s Operation Christmas Child drive. The deadline's Nov. 22. Williams Lake residents have until Sunday, Nov. 22 to drop off gift-filled shoeboxes at Evangelical Free Church for this year’s Operation Christmas Child drive. Kathy Shetler, a Williams Lake volunteer with Operation Christmas Child, has been involved since the mid 1990s when she began packing shoeboxes at Maranatha Christian School in Williams Lake. She has since helped lead the project locally, coordinate drop-offs and work with churches. Shetler said Williams Lake shipped 451 shoeboxes in 2025, with about 50 more donated online. She hopes to match or exceed last year’s in-person total. Operation Christmas Child is a Samaritan’s Purse project that works with local churches and ministries overseas to distribute gift-filled shoeboxes to children at Christian outreach events. Shetler suggested packing school supplies, hygiene items, a toy or craft kit and something to wear, such as a hat or gloves. Donors can choose to pack for a child ages two to four, five to nine or 10 to 14. Shetler asked donors to leave out candy, liquids, toothpaste, soap, glass items and war-themed toys. Shetler thanked Williams Lake residents for their generosity over the years. “It’s such an expression of love and compassion to children around the world that do not have much,” she said. Empty shoeboxes and brochures are available at the Evangelical Free Church, 1100 North 11th Ave., and at Kit and Kaboodle, 83A Second Ave. S. Filled shoeboxes can be dropped off at the church through Sunday, Nov. 22. Shetler said the boxes will travel through Kamloops to Calgary, where they’ll be checked before being shipped overseas.

The Revelstoke Grizzlies beat the Williams Lake Mustangs 4-1 at the Cariboo Memorial Recreation Complex on Saturday, Nov. 14, ending the Mustang's 12-game winning streak. The Williams Lake Mustangs’ 12 game winning streak ended Saturday with a home-ice loss against the Revelstoke Grizzlies. The Mustangs played back-to-back games against the Grizzlies on Nov. 13 and 14, splitting the series with both teams taking a win. During the first game, which was also played on home-ice, the Mustangs wore their throwback jerseys for Friday’s retro night and extended their winning streak to 12 games with a 5-2 victory. Logan Hauk opened the scoring with an unassisted goal, then set up Blake Collison alongside Declan Pocock. Pocock scored third goal off an assist from Hauk, giving Williams Lake a 3-0 lead heading into the first intermission. Hauk scored his second of the night 51 seconds into the middle frame, with assists from Chaz Lucas and Tristan Aidoo. Revelstoke’s Tayo Jackson answered with two power-play goals, cutting the Mustangs lead to 4-2. Braden Bolt sealed the win with an empty-net goal woth 30 seconds left in the third. Nolan Phare and Kaden Charpentier picked up the assists. Ivan Anderson stopped 26 of 28 shots for Williams Lake. Revelstoke starter Williams Stewart made six saves on eight shots, and Michael Makowsky stopped 32 of 33 in relief. Hauk finished with two goals and two assists, and he and Pocock were among the game’s three stars. During the next game on Nov. 14, The Revelstoke Grizzlies ended the Williams Lake Mustangs 12 game winning streak with a 4-1 victory. After a scoreless first period, the Grizzlies scored twice in the second before Kaden Charpentier cut the deficit to 2-1 with the Mustang’s only goal. 280c2b8932d514fc67c76b3c88797419.text: Five years behind bars and a restitution order for $800,000 was the sentence handed down to a Kelowna woman on Nov. 17 for fraud. Lorna Eng appeared before Justice Steven Wilson in Kelowna Supreme Court on the Tuesday afternoon to learn her fate. The woman was found guilty of fraud and theft over $5,000 by a jury, after taking $844,536.13 from her former employer, Nexus Dock and Marina, between 2015 and 2019 while working as the business manager and bookkeeper. Eng was found to have been diverting customer payments through online transfers to her personal bank account, diverting customer cheques to her personal bank account and issuing business cheques to herself using pre-signed cheques left in the company’s office for business use. It was also heard that Eng attempted to conceal the transactions by using different names and email addresses not recognized by her employers. The court heard that Eng’s fraudulent activity was not detected until an external accountant and bookkeeper was hired in 2019. Eng resigned from the company in May or June of that year. At trial, Eng argued that some transfers of money from Nexus into her account were under the direction of her employer to circumvent third parties, such as the Canada Revenue Agency. She also claimed police had failed to conduct a thorough investigation into all bank accounts and credit cards, including that of her employer, and that the prosecution had not proven the charges beyond a reasonable doubt. As a result of financial challenges, Nexus closed in 2019, selling off assets and laying off 12 employees. “He described the emotional toll to have been immense and he spent a lot of time trying to understand how these circumstances could have arisen,” Justice Wilson said about a victim impact statement provided by one of the business owners. dc56bb67037fa680f0226819b8fefe5f.text: A coordinated police response led to the arrest of a woman wanted in Alberta, driving at dangerous speeds through Greater Victoria, sometimes exceeding 180 km/h. According to Sidney/North Saanich RCMP, the incident occurred shortly before 1:30 a.m. on Nov. 14 when officers attempted to conduct an impaired driving check stop in North Saanich. The driver, identified as 34-year-old Jasmine Ann Scott, fled at high speed, said an RCMP news release. Because of public safety concerns, officers did not pursue Scott, instead immediately coordinating a response with neighbouring police agencies. “It is alleged the suspect vehicle travelled through several jurisdictions at dangerous speeds, at times exceeding 180 km/h,” police said. “Through a coordinated regional response involving Sidney/North Saanich RCMP, Central Saanich Police Service, and West Shore RCMP, officers monitored the vehicle, shared real-time information, and used automated licence plate recognition technology to locate it several hours later.” Using a tire deflation device, West Shore RCMP successfully brought the vehicle to a controlled stop on the Malahat Highway, shortly after 3:30 a.m. The vehicle’s two occupants were arrested without incident. Scott has been charged with dangerous driving and flight from police. She was also arrested on multiple outstanding Alberta warrants. Anyone who witnessed a white Nissan Rogue travelling at excessive speeds on Highway 17 or the Malahat Highway during the early morning hours of Nov. 14, and has not yet spoken with police, is asked to contact Sidney/North Saanich RCMP at 250-656-3931 and quote file 2026-5998.

c0df65c332ea90abf74eb5dd92bf1a94.text: Police in Nanaimo investigated after Yasin Khan was shot and killed there in May 2021. Ronald Joseph Campbell, 42, was subsequently arrested. The victim of a 2021 gangland slaying in Nanaimo was also the target of a previous attempt on his life just months before in Langley, a court heard earlier this month. On Nov. 4, Ronald Joseph Campbell, 42, was found guilty of first-degree murder in the May 20, 2021 killing of Yasin Khan. Khan was shot while parked in a BMW SUV outside a Wendy’s at a Nanaimo shopping centre. Justice Douglas Thompson said that while there was not enough evidence to say with certainty that Campbell had pulled the trigger, he was involved in aiding and facilitating the murder plot. It was the second time in five months that someone had tried to kill Khan, the court learned. As part of Thompson’s summary of the case, he noted that Khan was one of two men who ran from a bullet-riddled Dodge Durango on Jan. 30, 2021, in Langley. The Langley Advance Times reported at the time that the shooting took place around the 7000-block of 196A Street near the Langley-Surrey border, at around 7:30 p.m. Inside the Durango, police found drug-dealing paraphernalia, including multiple phones that were ringing with drug orders, according to Thompson’s summary. Both men who had been in the Durango survived unharmed, but they refused to help police, according to local investigators. The same man who had been with Khan during the Langley shooting was with him, in another car parked next to his, during the fatal shooting in Nanaimo. That man is not named in the court record. There was no indication whether the Langley shooting was directly linked to the Nanaimo shooting, or whether any of the same people were involved. Campbell, who was working for the Bacon Brothers gang in early 2021, has been sentenced to life in prison with no possibility of parole for 25 years, the automatic sentence for first-degree murder.

252f8b417262611be3a1ad36a2eeeb78.text: B.C. pop star Carly Rae Jepsen to host 2027 JUNO Awards | Williams Lake Tribune Mission's Carly Rae Jepsen will host and perform at the 2027 JUNO Awards in Winnipeg on April 4. Mission’s Carly Rae Jepsen is set to host the 2027 JUNO Awards in Winnipeg. The Canadian Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences (CARAS) and CBC announced Jepsen as host on Nov. 9, with the show scheduled for April 4 at Canada Life Centre. According to a news release, the three-time JUNO winner from Mission will bring her signature pop sound to the stage while leading the festivities as host for the first time. In addition to Jepsen, the show will feature performances from Angine De Poitrine, Our Lady Peace, and more. Allan Reid, the president/CEO of CARAS and the JUNO Awards, said the lineup brings together artists who have helped shape the sound of Canadian music alongside those pushing it in exciting new directions. “From celebrating the incredible legacy of Our Lady Peace to welcoming Carly Rae Jepsen as our host, we can’t wait to share these moments with fans in Winnipeg and across the country,” Reid said. Jepsen earned Album of the Year and Pop Album of the Year at the 2013 JUNO Awards for her 2012 album, *Kiss.* The hit “Call Me Maybe” took home Single of the Year at the same awards. In September, the Mission pop star released her 8th studio album, *Day and Night*. It included the singles “On Wire”, “Motivation”, and “Don’t Leave Me on the Dance Floor.” The 24-track double album was inspired by a period of personal transformation and reflects Jepsen’s continued creative evolution and willingness to explore new musical directions. Per the release, it explores two sides of her artistry, blending “sun-soaked, folk-leaning pop with after-hours dance music”. Jepsen’s “Day and Night Tour” kicks off over a week after the JUNOs, including a show at The Orpheum in Vancouver on April 18.

9d0fb319854b44cd96bc9386a0f773bc.text: Teck's mine at Highland Valley near Logan Lake is the largest open-pit copper mine in Canada. B.C.’s Labour Relations Board has partially sided with a union in its bid to seek remedies for non-bargaining workers doing the work of union members. Board vice-chair Paul Todd released his decision Friday (Nov. 13), following a four-day hearing between the United Steelworkers Local 7619 and Teck’s Highland Valley Copper mine. The United Steelworkers Local 7619 alleged Teck’s Highland Valley Copper was breaching two sections of the Labour Relations Code – sections 6(3)(e) and 68 – by using ineligible replacement workers and contractors to perform the work of employees who are currently on strike. The union represents 1,200 employees at the mine. The union initially claimed the employer breached code in seven instances, but following pre-hearing discussions, it was narrowed down to five instances. The union was seeking remedies that included a declaration, a cease-and-desist order, damages and an order to have a designated union representative access the worksite. Teck operates Highland Valley Copper mine, which is about 17 kilometres west of Logan Lake. The company began a large construction project in August 2025 to expand and extend the life of the mine. According to the decision, the project construction work is “largely” performed by contractors and not members of the bargaining unit. Teck and Local 7619’s collective agreement expired on Sept. 30. The union members voted in favour of a strike on Oct. 19, with job action beginning on Oct. 24. The project area, according to the decision, is a common site for picketing. Todd found Teck breached Section 68 of the Labour Relations Code by having three workers perform work meant to be done by bargaining employees, as well as having a contractor do some road work. d94f3bc87ca2114bbedefc6ca017afd3.text: Sgt. Freda Fong, with the Integrated Homicide Investigation Team (IHIT), announced the arrest of two people in a fatal shooting in September 2025 in Langley. Tushar Sharma was found dead in a burning car near Fort Langley in late October. Homicide investigators are asking for tips. Firefighters discovered human remains while investigating a vehicle fire in Fort Langley last month, and now homicide investigators have taken over the investigation. Tushar Sharma, a 25-year-old Surrey man, has been identified as the victim by the Integrated Homicide Investigation Team (IHIT). Sharma’s body was found on Oct. 29 when RCMP and firefighters responded to a report of a car on fire in the 23300-block of Rawlison Crescent. The site is just south of the village of Fort Langley in a rural area. The deceased man does not have a criminal record, and according to IHIT, he had limited known contacts in Canada. “IHIT investigators continue to work with Mr. Sharma’s family and friends in Canada and overseas to gain a better understanding of his lifestyle and activities leading up to his death,” said Sgt. Freda Fong, of IHIT. “While the motive remains under investigation, evidence to date suggests this was a targeted incident.” IHIT is working with the Langley RCMP and the Integrated Forensic Identification Services unit, along with the BC Coroners Service to determine what happened to Sharma. The homicide investigators are working to put together a timeline of the events leading up to Sharma’s death. Anyone with information is asked to contact IHIT at 1-877-551-IHIT (4448) or by email at ihitinfo@rcmp-grc.gc.ca.

aaa84fe4aae62506e240bbf9961dda9c.text: A 28-year-old man is facing multiple charges after Quesnel RCMP located a stolen pickup truck from Agassiz, B.C. According to an RCMP press release, at approximately 4:23 a.m. on Nov. 13, police located a stolen Doge Ram pickup truck in Quesnel. A man was seen fleeing from the vehicle in the 300-block of Doherty Drive. Officers located and arrested Kyle Fredrick Ford a short distance away. Mounties said Ford has been held in custody and charged with possession of stolen property, prohibited driving and two counts of failing to comply with conditions.

02f26c80dc370a7e9dad29172d470d51.text: Quesnel RCMP seized a handgun, thousands of dollars in cash and several suspected illegal drugs during the arrest of a 33-year-old man. According to an RCMP press release, Mounties arrested the man at approximately 4:15 p.m. on Nov. 12 in the 400-block of Willis Street in Quesnel. RCMP said during the arrest, officers seized a 9mm handgun, approximately $13,000 in cash, 102.7 grams of suspected fentanyl, 48 grams of suspected crack cocaine and 84 grams of methamphetamine as well as miscellaneous pills. Mounties said the man has since been released pending further investigation.

The youngest contributor to the River of Recovery mural was about five and a half months old. Her mother added a tiny footprint. Several elders in their 80s also contributed. The opening day began with a community march and candlelight vigil, and the final day’s event included naloxone training. The local week programming took place ahead of National Addictions Awareness Week, which runs from Nov. 15 to Nov. 21 across Canada. Over the five days, WLFN hosted workshops, community gatherings, wellness services, and recovery activities. 1f8430898597dae8f01640ef53bf1b58.text: Chad Marchand was among the vendors at last Saturday's Made in the Cariboo Christmas Market with his custom hardwood cutting boards. It was everything locally made at the Williams Lake Tourism Discovery Centre on Saturday, Nov. 14 where the annual Made in the Cariboo Christmas Market was held. More than 700 people filtered in to explore 28 vendors set up on all three floors offering a variety of wares. New this year was Chad Marchand of Williams Lake with his custom hardwood cutting boards. The professional forester with BC Timber Sales handcrafts the end grain boards in a small shop in his family’s backyard where they are also sealed with beeswax. “I wanted one for my own brisket making,” Marchand said with a laugh, adding he still doesn’t have one for himself just yet. “Every time one comes out I can’t decide this is the one for me so I just keep on making them.” It has been approximately five to six months that Marchand has started making his unique cutting boards that he typically does after work along his other hobby, gardening. Tourism Discovery Centre operations manager and Williams Lake and District Chamber of Commerce executive assistant Tanya Hutchison called Made in the Cariboo Christmas Market a great way to bring local vendors and showcase their artisan skills with the community. Their products also might not be necessarily found in any other store. Marchand hopes to participate in other upcoming local holiday markets and has already signed up to be part of next year’s Made in the Cariboo Christmas Market.

Tŝilhqot’in ʔEten Nadiltil, TEN, a majority Indigenous owned construction company, has partnered with Kamloops based Dawson Civil to expand its civil construction and infrastructure operations across B.C. Dandzen Development LP, the economic development arm of the Tŝilhqot’in National Government, founded TEN in 2017 and hold a 51 per cent stake in the company. In a media release, TEN board director Dalton Baptiste said the company was founded to make roads safer in Tŝilhqot’in territory and help diversify the local economy amid a downturn in forestry. He said TEN now aims to work with Indigenous communities and businesses across B.C. on large infrastructure projects that create jobs and business opportunities for Tŝilhqot’inpeople. This new partnership bring together Indigenous leadership and over a century of experience in complex infrastructure, mining, and industrial environments. Tŝilhqot’in National Government represents the six Tŝilhqot’in in communities: Tl’etinqox, ʔEsdilagh, Yuneŝit’in, Tŝideldel, Tl’esqox, and Xeni Gwet’in. Baptiste added in the media release “That vision has not changed, it has only expanded. We are growing a company that will continue to create lasting employment and business opportunities for our people and redefine what Indigenous-led enterprise looks like in British Columbia.” He added, “Our goal is to partner with Indigenous communities and companies across the province to deliver large-scale infrastructure projects that benefit all British Columbians with respect for the land and Tŝilhqot’in values always guiding our work.” TEN’s work includes earthworks, regional and municipal infrastructure, and mining construction. The company also serves the forestry, mining, energy, civil and municipal, industrial, and road maintenance sectors. ccee08dc4d9b2794e28f9893f2ef6cc7.text: Students can browse graduation outfits at Ever After Attire's Borrowed Magic pop-up in Williams Lake on Nov. 21 and borrow an outfit for free. Williams Lake students looking for something to wear to graduation can try on dresses and suits and take an outfit home for free at Ever After Attire’s Borrowed Magic pop-up. The drop-in event runs from 12 p.m. to 3 p.m. on Saturday, Nov. 21, in the Graham Kelsey Room at the Central Cariboo Arts and Culture Centre. Admission is free and no registration is required. Nikki Blodgett, program coordinator for Ever After Attire remembers looking for a graduation dress when she was in high school. “Shopping for a grad dress was so expensive and I wondered how everyone could do it,” Blodgett said. She took over the program from Williams Lake photographer Rick Magnell and has been running it for about a year. Ever After Attire’s lending program is open to graduates in the Williams Lake area regardless of financial circumstances. Blodgett said the collection includes about 125 dresses, along with suits, dress pants, shirts, ties, dress shoes and heels. A change room will be available, and students can bring a friend or parent to help with fittings. Volunteers can also help students choose an outfit or lace up a dress. Ever After Attire said seamstress Dominique Bouchard will be on hand to help with small fixes, such as loose straps or fasteners, and offer advice on alterations. Students who find an outfit they want to borrow can leave their name and phone number and take it home that day. Dresses and suits are due back to Cariboo Corner within two weeks after graduation. Wanda Ranson from Dream Day Bouquet Floral Design will be offering a free floral-themed craft, and Sparkle Booth will provide free photos. Permanent jewellery will also be available for a fee by appointment, Blodgett said. Now in its third year, the DIY poppy workshop in Williams Lake brings people together to turn reclaimed fabrics into poppies, share family stories and honour those who served ahead of Remembrance Day. Materials from the Salvation Army thrift store find new life as handmade poppies during the third annual up cycled poppy workshop at NEXT GENeral in Williams Lake. d3f8ec8166909cda31f3692d79e0e82a.text: Anti-SOGI Protesters and pro-SOGI counter-protesters took to the streets in Vancouver on Wednesday, Sept. 20, 2023. During the provincial election campaign’s home stretch in late October, premier-designate Lorne Doerkson held a boisterous rally in a Surrey warehouse, hitting his major talking points to thunderous approval. One of the biggest applause lines came when he mentioned the B.C. schools initiative called Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity 123. “We are going to get our grades up, and we are going to repeal SOGI!” Doerkson shouted. SOGI 123 is a set of resources provided by an organization called the ARC Foundation to help teachers talk about sexual orientation and gender with students, with the goal being to reduce stigma and bullying. It is sometimes mistakenly referred to as a curriculum and confused with sex education, which it is not. Christy Clark’s B.C. Liberal government created it via a ministerial directive in 2016, and over the past 10 years SOGI-inclusive learning has been threaded into the education system. (Clark sat ringside at Doerkson’s Surrey rally, cheering him on.) As a set of educational resources rather than a law, SOGI 123 is not technically subject to repeal. So what could Doerkson mean in practice when he says he wants to repeal SOGI? And how will schools continue to work to protect gender-diverse students from bullying and harassment? This past summer, the B.C. government ended its partnership with ARC, leading the foundation to wind down operations. In some sense, this means that the province’s schools have already moved beyond SOGI 123. In a news release, then-Conservative Party leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay and the party’s education critic at the time, Lynne Block, hailed the termination of the ARC partnership as the “end of SOGI.” According to B.C. c99cecf48a644b68453a76c90064410a.text: Fundraising target set at $3.5M for robotic surgical system for B.C. hospital | Williams Lake Tribune Fundraising target set at $3.5M for robotic surgical system for B.C. hospital Nanaimo and District Hospital Foundation wants to raise $3.5 million to bring a da Vinci Surgical System to Nanaimo Regional General Hospital. Various images of the da Vinci Surgical System Nanaimo and District Hospital Foundation wants to bring to the hospital in Nanaimo. A non-profit intends to bring the first surgical robotic system to Nanaimo Regional General Hospital for more precise surgeries. In a press release, Nanaimo and District Hospital Foundation says it hopes to raise $3.5 million in its 2026/27 winter fundraising drive for the da Vinci Surgical System for use at NRGH – it would be the first robotics program in Nanaimo and the second on Vancouver Island. A “robotic-assisted surgical platform,” the system utilizes a doctor’s hand motions, translating them “into precise, real-time movements of miniaturized instruments inside the body,” according to the press release. “It combines high-definition 3-D visualization, instruments with greater range of motion than the human hand, and advanced features to support highly precise, minimally invasive surgery,” it noted. Robotic-assisted surgery has become the norm for care in hospitals across the continent and affords hospital personnel the ability to “operate with enhanced precision, visualization and control through smaller incisions, including in areas of the body that can be difficult to reach using conventional surgical instruments.” At first, the da Vinci Surgical System will be utilized for procedures such as those for kidneys, colorectal and prostates, with intention to add ear-nose-throat surgery and gynecology, in the future. Supreme Court judge dismissed a defamation lawsuit brought forward by the former mayor of Quesnel’s wife against a city councillor over comments made during a 2024 council meeting. In a decision published on Nov. 10, Justice Tindale ruled that Quesnel Coun. Laurey-Anne Roodenburg’s statements about Pat Morton’s distribution of a book questioning the findings surrounding residential schools were protected under the Protection of Public Participation Act. Morton, the wife of former Quesnel Mayor Ron Paull, filed the lawsuit following comments Roodenburg made during a March 19, 2024, council meeting. According to the court document, the controversy began after Morton distributed copies of _Grave Error: How the Media Misled Us (and the Truth about Residential Schools),_ which she had purchased in February 2024. On March 19, 2024, Lhtako Dene Nation sent a letter to the mayor and council expressing concern about the book, saying it questioned the existence of residential schools and whether cultural genocide had occurred. The letter called on council to reaffirm its Memorandum of Understanding with the Nation and offered to have Elders who attended residential schools share first-hand knowledge of their experiences with council. According to the court document, during the meeting in March, Paull identified his wife as the person distributing the book and said he had not read it. NDP calls for opposition to Quebecor’s Telus takeover bid The Telus Park building on 64 Avenue in Surrey, pictured on Nov. 18, 2026. Interim B.C. NDP Leader Jennifer Whiteside is calling on the incoming government to oppose Quebecor’s $31-billion bid to take over Telus, warning it would reduce competition and could lead to higher prices for British Columbians. “Consolidating two major national telecommunications players will inevitably reduce competition in our market, leading to fewer choices, diminished service quality, and higher monthly bills for families and small businesses,” Whiteside said in a letter addressed to incoming premier Lorne Doerkson. Telus is B.C. based, while Quebecor is headquartered in Montreal. Both companies compete in B.C.’s budget cell-phone market: Telus owns Public Mobile, and Quebecor owns Freedom Mobile. In addition to reducing competition, Whiteside says the shift to East Coast ownership would be bad for B.C.’s economy. Telus is headquartered in Vancouver and has multiple new office buildings under construction. “For decades, Telus has been a cornerstone of British Columbia’s technology and telecommunications sector,” she said. “The prospect of an out-of-province acquisition raises serious concerns for working families, businesses, and our provincial economy.” The takeover bid, which offers cash and shares, would still need regulatory approval. Quebecor argues it would create a “strong pan-Canadian competitor” to compete with other national providers and foreign competitors. Doerkson responded to Whiteside’s letter by saying he wants to ensure British Columbians have choice, competitive prices and reliable cell service. He also wants local jobs preserved. “There are legitimate questions raised by a change in ownership and must be fully considered as part of any approval process,” he said in a written statement.
